<reason>Both sides ran coherent, well-grounded cases with real clash. CON landed the sharpest single lines ("voice without detection is just screaming into a recorder," the chef/menu weighing) and effectively flipped Flint and the Weimar mechanism-parasitism point. But PRO controlled the motion's core question across all rounds: competence is always measured against a target it cannot choose, and B never named a non-democratic authority entitled to set ends — instead conceding in B4.1 that the public may revoke any insulated mandate with no overriding body. PRO's closing converted that concession into the decisive advice-vs-authority distinction, which CON's "paper ownership, not correctness" and burning-building reframes never fully erased. PRO also re-flipped Flint (appointed manager overriding an elected council; voice supplied the demand, accountability the fix) and answered both pressure questions directly and in format, while CON's second rebuttal was clipped for exceeding the word limit — a real execution cost. CON's necessity-vs-importance pushback ("a poor one" government, selector vs. chef) kept it close, but PRO answered the most pressure with cleaner execution and the clearer reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The delegation/revocation thread: B4.1's "revocability proves who holds the paper, not who is right" was the single sharpest blow, but PRO's closing flipped CON's own concession — the public may revoke and nothing overrules the legislature — into "advice ranks below authority," the exchange that ultimately decided the debate.</best_rebuttal>
